high_yield_leaves.question: In any agentic loop, what are the steps of a single iteration from sending a request to sending the next one, and which single field decides whether the loop continues?
answer_slot: lists send request -> read stop_reason -> if tool_use execute tools -> append results -> resend
identifies stop_reason as the sole continuation signal
names the request-shaping fields the loop sets per request: max_tokens and the system prompt

high_yield_leaves.question: A teammate proposes ending the loop when the assistant's text contains 'TASK COMPLETE' - what makes this an anti-pattern, and what should signal completion instead?
answer_slot: natural-language signals are probabilistic and phrasing-dependent - the model may omit or emit them spuriously
stop_reason end_turn is the structured, reliable completion signal

high_yield_leaves.question: Why can a subagent not simply 'know' what the coordinator or a sibling learned earlier, and what does that force the coordinator to do?
answer_slot: subagents run with isolated context - no automatic inheritance of coordinator history or sibling results
coordinator must explicitly route needed information into each subagent's prompt
forgetting this yields subagents that redo work or answer generically

high_yield_leaves.question: Every subagent in a research pipeline succeeded, yet the final report covers only a narrow slice of the topic - where do you look first for the root cause and why?
answer_slot: look at the coordinator's task decomposition - the subtasks it assigned define maximum possible coverage
subagents executing narrow assignments correctly cannot recover breadth that was never assigned
blaming search queries, analysis filters, or synthesis instructions misreads correct downstream behavior

high_yield_leaves.question: A coordinator's Task tool calls silently never spawn anything - what configuration must you check first, and what is the general rule it instantiates?
answer_slot: check that 'Task' is included in the coordinator's allowedTools
rule: subagent spawning is itself a tool call and is gated by tool permissions like any other

high_yield_leaves.question: A synthesis subagent produces generic output that ignores the search results gathered minutes earlier - what is the most likely cause and the fix?
answer_slot: cause: findings were never placed in its prompt - subagents do not inherit parent context or share memory between invocations
fix: include the complete prior-agent findings (search results, analysis outputs) directly in the synthesis prompt

high_yield_leaves.question: An agent skips identity verification before financial operations in a small percent of cases despite a mandatory-sounding system prompt - why is more prompting (or few-shot examples) the wrong fix, and what is the right one?
answer_slot: prompt and few-shot compliance is probabilistic; any non-zero failure rate is unacceptable when errors have financial consequences
right fix: programmatic prerequisite that blocks the downstream tools until verification returns a verified ID
distinguishes tool-ordering problems from tool-availability problems (routing classifiers solve the wrong problem)

high_yield_leaves.question: What must a structured handoff summary contain when escalating mid-process to a human agent, and why is each field there?
answer_slot: customer ID (so the human can act without re-identification)
root cause analysis and refund amount / findings so far (so investigation is not repeated)
recommended action (so the human starts from a decision, not from zero)

high_yield_leaves.question: Three MCP tools return timestamps as Unix epoch, ISO 8601, and locale strings, and the agent keeps mis-comparing dates - where do you normalize and why there?
answer_slot: implement a PostToolUse hook that converts all formats to one canonical form before the model processes results
normalizing in the hook is deterministic; asking the model to convert in-prompt fails intermittently
fixing each tool server may be impossible (third-party) - the hook is your integration boundary

high_yield_leaves.question: How do you make it impossible - not just unlikely - for an agent to process a refund above a policy threshold, and why can no system prompt achieve this?
answer_slot: implement a tool-call interception hook that blocks process_refund calls exceeding the threshold
prompts yield probabilistic compliance with a non-zero violation rate - unacceptable for hard policy
the hook runs in code, outside anything the model can talk itself around

high_yield_leaves.question: What properties of a workflow tell you to use a fixed prompt chain versus dynamic decomposition, and what breaks when you pick wrong?
answer_slot: fixed chain: steps known in advance and stable across instances (e.g. per-aspect review passes)
dynamic: next steps depend on intermediate findings (e.g. open-ended investigation)
wrong-fixed breaks on surprises; wrong-dynamic adds cost and nondeterminism to routine work

high_yield_leaves.question: A single-pass review of a large multi-file change gives detailed feedback on some files, superficial on others, and contradicts itself - what restructuring fixes it and what is the root cause?
answer_slot: root cause: attention dilution when analyzing many files at once
fix: per-file passes for local issues plus a separate integration pass for cross-file flow
bigger context windows do not fix attention quality; consensus voting suppresses real findings

high_yield_leaves.question: After major code changes, why is starting a new session with a structured summary more reliable than resuming the old one, and what goes into the summary?
answer_slot: resumed stale tool results describe code that no longer exists - the model reasons from fiction
fresh session + injected structured summary carries forward conclusions without stale evidence
summary holds key findings and decisions, not raw tool output

high_yield_leaves.question: You want to compare two testing strategies that both depend on the same expensive codebase analysis - what mechanism do you use and why not two fresh sessions or one shared session?
answer_slot: fork_session twice from the analysis baseline - each strategy explored in its own branch
two fresh sessions duplicate the analysis cost and may diverge in their understanding
one shared session lets the strategies contaminate each other's reasoning

high_yield_leaves.question: Users ask about orders and the agent calls get_customer instead of lookup_order; both have one-line descriptions - what is the most effective first step and why is it first?
answer_slot: expand each description: input formats handled, example queries, edge cases, boundaries versus the similar tool
descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for selection - minimal ones are the root cause
first because low-effort/high-leverage: few-shot adds tokens without fixing the cause; routing layers and tool consolidation are heavier redesigns

high_yield_leaves.question: analyze_content and analyze_document have near-identical descriptions and get misrouted constantly - what rename-and-describe move fixes it, and what makes a name self-disambiguating?
answer_slot: rename to reflect the actual domain, e.g. analyze_content -> extract_web_results with a web-specific description
self-disambiguating: the name itself encodes the input domain or action so overlap disappears at a glance
name and description must agree - a good name with a generic description still misroutes

high_yield_leaves.question: What does a well-structured MCP tool error response contain, and what does the isError flag itself communicate?
answer_slot: isError flag marks the result as a failure the agent must reason about (MCP's failure-communication pattern)
errorCategory (transient/validation/permission), isRetryable boolean, human-readable description
each field maps to a distinct agent decision: what happened, whether to retry, what to say

high_yield_leaves.question: A search returns nothing - how must the tool distinguish 'no matches exist' from 'could not access the source', and what wrong behavior follows from conflating them?
answer_slot: valid empty result = successful query with zero matches; access failure = error needing a retry decision
conflation as failure triggers pointless retries of a correct answer
conflation as success silently drops recoverable data from the research

high_yield_leaves.question: A synthesis agent needs frequent simple fact-checks but full search access violates its role; round-tripping through the coordinator adds 40% latency - what design resolves this, and why not the extremes?
answer_slot: give it a scoped verify_fact tool for the high-frequency simple case
complex verifications still delegate through the coordinator to the search agent
full search access over-provisions and violates separation of concerns; batching creates blocking dependencies; speculative caching cannot predict needs

high_yield_leaves.question: Which options does tool_choice offer, and exactly what behavior does each permit or compel?
answer_slot: auto: tool calls optional - the model may respond with plain text
any: a tool call is compulsory but the model chooses which tool
forced {type:'tool', name:'...'}: that specific tool must be called

high_yield_leaves.question: A team-shared MCP server and a personal experimental one - which config file does each belong in, and what property of each file makes it the right home?
answer_slot: team-shared: project-scoped .mcp.json - version-controlled, so the whole team gets it
personal/experimental: user-scoped ~/.claude.json - private, no teammate impact
the scope decision is exactly the sharing decision

high_yield_leaves.question: The agent keeps using built-in Grep instead of your far more capable MCP search tool - why, and what is the fix?
answer_slot: the MCP tool's description undersells it - the agent cannot know the capability advantage
enhance the description to explain capabilities and outputs in detail
selection is description-driven; built-ins win ties by familiarity

high_yield_leaves.question: What precisely is the Grep/Glob discrimination - what does each search over, and which one task is each uniquely right for?
answer_slot: Grep: file contents - patterns like function names, error messages, import statements
Glob: file paths - names and extension patterns
find all callers of a function -> Grep; find all *.test.tsx files -> Glob

high_yield_leaves.question: Edit keeps failing because your anchor text appears multiple times in the file - what is the reliable fallback procedure?
answer_slot: Read the full file contents, apply the modification, then Write the complete updated file
Read+Write does not depend on anchor uniqueness
this is the documented fallback when unique anchors cannot be found

high_yield_leaves.question: A new team member's Claude Code ignores conventions everyone else gets - what misplacement explains it and what is the fix?
answer_slot: the conventions live in someone's user-level ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which is not shared via version control
fix: move team-wide instructions to project-level CLAUDE.md committed to the repo
general law: sharing scope is determined by which level holds the instruction

high_yield_leaves.question: Your CLAUDE.md mixes testing, API, and deployment guidance and has become unmanageable - what reorganization does Claude Code support and what does each resulting file look like?
answer_slot: split into focused topic files in .claude/rules/ (testing.md, api-conventions.md, deployment.md)
each file carries one coherent concern, independently maintainable
this replaces the monolithic CLAUDE.md pattern for large rule sets

high_yield_leaves.question: A /review command must be available to every developer the moment they clone or pull the repo - where does the file go, and why do the plausible alternatives fail?
answer_slot: create it in .claude/commands/ inside the repository - version control distributes it
~/.claude/commands/ is personal and unshared; CLAUDE.md holds instructions, not command definitions
no commands array in a config JSON exists

high_yield_leaves.question: A codebase-analysis skill floods the main conversation with exploratory output - which frontmatter option fixes it, and what exactly changes at runtime?
answer_slot: context: fork - the skill runs in an isolated sub-agent context
verbose/exploratory output stays in the fork; only results return to the main session
same option applies to brainstorming skills whose exploration should not persist

high_yield_leaves.question: Write the skeleton of a path-scoped rule file for Terraform conventions - what frontmatter field and value make it conditional?
answer_slot: a .claude/rules/ file with YAML frontmatter containing paths: ["terraform/**/*"]
the body holds the conventions; the paths globs are the activation condition

high_yield_leaves.question: Test files sit next to the code they test all over the repo, and all tests must share conventions - which mechanism applies them automatically and why does each alternative fail?
answer_slot: .claude/rules/ file with a glob like **/*.test.tsx - matches by path pattern regardless of directory
directory CLAUDE.md files are directory-bound and cannot follow scattered files
root-CLAUDE.md headers rely on inference; skills require invocation - neither is deterministic automatic application

high_yield_leaves.question: Restructuring a monolith into microservices touches dozens of files and demands service-boundary decisions - which mode and what does it buy before any change is made?
answer_slot: plan mode - the task has large scale, architectural decisions, and multiple valid approaches
buys safe exploration of the codebase and dependency understanding before committing
prevents costly rework from late-discovered dependencies

high_yield_leaves.question: Adding a single date-validation conditional to one function - which mode, and what would the other mode cost you here?
answer_slot: direct execution - simple, well-scoped, one file, clear change
plan mode here adds ceremony and latency with nothing to de-risk
scoping clarity, not file count alone, is the criterion

high_yield_leaves.question: Your prose description of a data transformation yields different behavior each attempt - what do you add, how many, and why does it work?
answer_slot: provide 2-3 concrete input/output examples of the expected transformation
examples pin down semantics that prose leaves ambiguous
this is the most effective communication when descriptions are interpreted inconsistently

high_yield_leaves.question: You have several issues to fix - what determines whether you present them all in one detailed message or fix them one at a time?
answer_slot: interacting problems: one message, so fixes are designed jointly and do not conflict
independent problems: sequential iteration keeps each round focused and verifiable
misbatching costs either conflicting patches or needless round-trips

high_yield_leaves.question: A pipeline running claude "analyze this PR" hangs forever - what is happening, what flag fixes it, and which folk remedies fail?
answer_slot: Claude Code is waiting for interactive input; the -p (--print) flag runs it non-interactively
-p processes the prompt, writes to stdout, and exits - what CI requires
CLAUDE_HEADLESS and --batch do not exist; stdin redirection does not address the interaction model

high_yield_leaves.question: Your CI must post review findings as inline PR comments automatically - which CLI flags produce output a script can rely on, and what does each contribute?
answer_slot: --output-format json makes the output machine-parseable
--json-schema constrains the JSON to your findings schema
together they turn free text into a stable automation contract

high_yield_leaves.question: You added 'be conservative and only report high-confidence findings' and the false positive rate did not move - why do such instructions fail, and what class of instruction works?
answer_slot: confidence-based filtering gives the model no operational definition of what to skip
specific categorical criteria work: report bugs and security issues, skip minor style and local patterns
the model needs category boundaries, not a dial for a confidence it cannot calibrate

high_yield_leaves.question: One review category produces mostly noise and developers have started dismissing everything - what is the immediate move and what is its exit condition?
answer_slot: temporarily disable the high false-positive categories
keep accurate categories running so trust can rebuild on real signal
re-enable a category once its improved prompt demonstrates acceptable precision

high_yield_leaves.question: Detailed instructions still yield inconsistently formatted, hit-or-miss output - what technique do you reach for, with how many examples, targeted at what?
answer_slot: add few-shot examples - the most effective technique for consistent, actionable output
2-4 targeted examples, not a large pile
target the ambiguous scenarios where behavior actually diverges

high_yield_leaves.question: Extraction returns empty/null for required fields that ARE present in oddly formatted documents - what is the few-shot fix and why does it also reduce hallucination?
answer_slot: add examples showing correct extraction from documents with varied formats (informal measurements, unusual layouts)
the model learns to recognize the information despite surface variation
demonstrated grounded extraction reduces both misses and fabricated values

high_yield_leaves.question: What precisely may and must the model do under tool_choice auto, any, and forced - and in which one situation is each the right setting?
answer_slot: auto: may call a tool or answer in text - right for genuinely optional tool use
any: must call some tool, model picks which - right when structure is mandatory but the schema choice is the model's
forced {type:'tool',name:...}: must call that tool - right when one specific extraction must run

high_yield_leaves.question: The model keeps inventing plausible values for fields the source document simply lacks - which schema decision causes this and what is the fix?
answer_slot: cause: the fields are marked required, forcing a value to satisfy the schema
fix: make such fields optional/nullable so absence is representable
rule: schema optionality must mirror real-world availability of the information

high_yield_leaves.question: Which validation failures will retries never fix no matter how good the feedback, and what signal tells you to stop retrying?
answer_slot: failures where the required information is simply absent from the provided source (e.g. exists only in an external document)
signal: the error is about missing information, not about format or structure
correct response: route to a different remedy (get the source, mark null, human review) instead of burning retries

high_yield_leaves.question: Developers dismiss many review findings and you want to fix the prompt systematically rather than anecdotally - what field do you add to each finding and what analysis does it unlock?
answer_slot: add a detected_pattern field recording which code construct triggered the finding
dismissals can then be aggregated by pattern to reveal systematic false-positive sources
prompt fixes target measured patterns instead of vibes

high_yield_leaves.question: A manager proposes moving both a blocking pre-merge check and an overnight tech-debt report to the Batch API for cost savings - what is the correct split and the deciding property?
answer_slot: batch the overnight report; keep the pre-merge check synchronous
deciding property: batch has no latency SLA and can take up to 24 hours - unacceptable where developers block
'usually faster' is not a guarantee; matching API to latency requirement beats uniform migration

high_yield_leaves.question: A batch returns with some items failed - what do you resubmit, how do you know which items those are, and what do you change on resubmission?
answer_slot: resubmit only the failed documents, not the whole batch
identify them via their custom_id correlation fields
modify per failure cause - e.g. chunk documents that exceeded context limits

high_yield_leaves.question: Why does the session that generated code systematically miss its own subtle bugs even when told to 'review carefully' or given extended thinking, and what architecture fixes it?
answer_slot: the generation session retains its reasoning context - it re-justifies rather than questions its decisions
self-review instructions and extended thinking do not remove that bias
fix: a second independent Claude instance reviewing without the generator's reasoning context

high_yield_leaves.question: A single-pass review of a 14-file PR gives uneven depth, misses obvious bugs, and contradicts itself between files - what restructuring fixes it and why do bigger contexts or majority voting not?
answer_slot: split into per-file passes for local issues plus a separate integration-focused pass for cross-file data flow
root cause is attention dilution - larger context windows do not restore attention quality
majority-of-three voting suppresses intermittently-caught real bugs; splitting PRs shifts burden to developers

high_yield_leaves.question: After progressive summarization, the agent misquotes the refund amount and promised dates - what got lost, and what structure prevents it?
answer_slot: summaries condensed exact numbers, dates, and customer-stated expectations into vague prose
extract transactional facts (amounts, dates, order numbers, statuses) into a persistent case-facts block
the block rides in every prompt outside the summarized history, immune to compression

high_yield_leaves.question: Findings from the middle of a long aggregated input keep getting omitted - what is the effect called, what are the two structural mitigations, and what must subagent outputs carry for synthesis to stay accurate?
answer_slot: the lost-in-the-middle effect: beginning and end process reliably, middles get dropped
mitigate: key-findings summary at the beginning, detailed results organized with explicit section headers
subagent outputs must include metadata (dates, source locations, methodological context) so downstream synthesis stays accurate

high_yield_leaves.question: First-contact resolution is far below target: the agent escalates straightforward damage claims yet attempts policy-exception cases alone - what fix addresses the root cause, and why do confidence thresholds, trained classifiers, and sentiment routing all miss it?
answer_slot: root cause: unclear decision boundaries - add explicit escalation criteria with few-shot escalate-vs-resolve examples to the system prompt
self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated (the agent is already wrongly confident); classifiers are over-engineering before prompt optimization is tried
sentiment tracks emotion, not case complexity - a different variable entirely

high_yield_leaves.question: get_customer returns three plausible matches - what must the agent do, and why is picking the best-looking match an anti-pattern?
answer_slot: ask the customer for additional identifiers to disambiguate
heuristic selection risks acting on the wrong account - misdirected refunds and privacy exposure
clarification is the required response to identity ambiguity

high_yield_leaves.question: A web-search subagent times out mid-research - what exactly should it return to the coordinator, and what recovery option does each element unlock?
answer_slot: failure type (what happened) -> retry-vs-abandon; attempted query -> retry with modification
partial results -> proceed with what exists; potential alternatives -> redirect strategy
the payload is designed backward from the coordinator's decision space

high_yield_leaves.question: What are the two opposite error-propagation anti-patterns, and what is the disciplined middle path between them, including who retries what?
answer_slot: anti-pattern 1: returning empty results marked successful - suppression prevents any recovery and corrupts outputs
anti-pattern 2: propagating the exception to kill the entire workflow when recovery could succeed
middle: local recovery for transient failures; propagate only unresolvables, with what was attempted and partial results

high_yield_leaves.question: An hour into exploration, the agent starts describing 'typical repository patterns' instead of the specific classes it actually found earlier - what is happening and what two immediate mechanisms respond?
answer_slot: context degradation: the specifics have effectively fallen out of usable context
reference the scratchpad of recorded findings to re-ground answers
/compact to reduce context consumed by verbose discovery output

high_yield_leaves.question: Design crash recovery for a long multi-agent exploration - what does each agent export, what does the coordinator load on resume, and where does recovered state go?
answer_slot: each agent exports structured state to a known location as it works
on resume the coordinator loads a manifest of that state
recovered state is injected into agent prompts so work resumes rather than restarts

high_yield_leaves.question: The system shows 97% aggregate accuracy and leadership wants to drop human review - what is wrong with the number, and what analysis must precede any reduction?
answer_slot: aggregates can hide failing segments - one document type or field may be far below 97%
analyze accuracy by document type and by field to verify consistent performance across all segments
automate only segments individually proven, not the average

high_yield_leaves.question: Raw model confidence scores cannot be trusted as thresholds - what turns them into a usable routing signal, at what granularity?
answer_slot: have the model output field-level confidence scores (not one blob per document)
calibrate review thresholds using labeled validation sets
calibration maps raw scores to observed error rates - the score becomes meaningful only through it

high_yield_leaves.question: Final reports contain claims nobody can trace to a source though every subagent cited carefully - where was attribution lost, and what output contract prevents it?
answer_slot: lost in summarization/synthesis steps that compressed findings without carrying claim-source mappings
contract: subagents emit structured claim-source mappings (source URLs, document names, relevant excerpts)
downstream agents are required to preserve and merge the mappings through every synthesis step

high_yield_leaves.question: Two credible sources report different values for the same statistic - what does the analysis agent do with them, and who reconciles?
answer_slot: complete the analysis with BOTH values included and the conflict explicitly annotated with source attribution
never arbitrarily select one value
the coordinator decides how to reconcile before passing to synthesis

sample_questions.stem: Production data shows that in 12% of cases, your agent skips get_customer entirely and calls lookup_order using only the customer's stated name, occasionally leading to misidentified accounts and incorrect refunds. What change would most effectively address this reliability issue?

options.A: Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order and process_refund calls until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
options.B: Enhance the system prompt to state that customer verification via get_customer is mandatory before any order operations.
options.C: Add few-shot examples showing the agent always calling get_customer first, even when customers volunteer order details.
options.D: Implement a routing classifier that analyzes each request and enables only the subset of tools appropriate for that request type.

sample_questions.rationale: When a specific tool sequence is required for critical business logic (like verifying customer identity before processing refunds), programmatic enforcement provides deterministic guarantees that prompt-based approaches cannot. Options B and C rely on probabilistic LLM compliance, which is insufficient when errors have financial consequences. Option D addresses tool availability rather than tool ordering, which is not the actual problem.

sample_questions.stem: Production logs show the agent frequently calls get_customer when users ask about orders (e.g., "check my order #12345"), instead of calling lookup_order. Both tools have minimal descriptions ("Retrieves customer information" / "Retrieves order details") and accept similar identifier formats. What's the most effective first step to improve tool selection reliability?

options.A: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt demonstrating correct tool selection patterns, with 5-8 examples showing order-related queries routing to lookup_order.
options.B: Expand each tool's description to include input formats it handles, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries explaining when to use it versus similar tools.
options.C: Implement a routing layer that parses user input before each turn and pre-selects the appropriate tool based on detected keywords and identifier patterns.
options.D: Consolidate both tools into a single lookup_entity tool that accepts any identifier and internally determines which backend to query.

sample_questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary mechanism LLMs use for tool selection. When descriptions are minimal, models lack the context to differentiate between similar tools. Option B directly addresses this root cause with a low-effort, high-leverage fix. Few-shot examples (A) add token overhead without fixing the underlying issue. A routing layer (C) is over-engineered and bypasses the LLM's natural language understanding. Consolidating tools (D) is a valid architectural choice but requires more effort than a "first step" warrants when the immediate problem is inadequate descriptions.

sample_questions.stem: Your agent achieves 55% first-contact resolution, well below the 80% target. Logs show it escalates straightforward cases (standard damage replacements with photo evidence) while attempting to autonomously handle complex situations requiring policy exceptions. What's the most effective way to improve escalation calibration?

options.A: Add explicit escalation criteria to your system prompt with few-shot examples demonstrating when to escalate versus resolve autonomously.
options.B: Have the agent self-report a confidence score (1-10) before each response and automatically route requests to humans when confidence falls below a threshold.
options.C: Deploy a separate classifier model trained on historical tickets to predict which requests need escalation before the main agent begins processing.
options.D: Implement sentiment analysis to detect customer frustration levels and automatically escalate when negative sentiment exceeds a threshold.

sample_questions.rationale: Adding explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples directly addresses the root cause: unclear decision boundaries. This is the proportionate first response before adding infrastructure. Option B fails because LLM self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated—the agent is already incorrectly confident on hard cases. Option C is over-engineered, requiring labeled data and ML infrastructure when prompt optimization hasn't been tried. Option D solves a different problem entirely; sentiment doesn't correlate with case complexity, which is the actual issue.

sample_questions.stem: You want to create a custom /review slash command that runs your team's standard code review checklist. This command should be available to every developer when they clone or pull the repository. Where should you create this command file?

options.A: In the .claude/commands/ directory in the project repository
options.B: In ~/.claude/commands/ in each developer's home directory
options.C: In the CLAUDE.md file at the project root
options.D: In a .claude/config.json file with a commands array

sample_questions.rationale: Project-scoped custom slash commands should be stored in the .claude/commands/ directory within the repository. These commands are version-controlled and automatically available to all developers when they clone or pull the repo. Option B (~/.claude/commands/) is for personal commands that aren't shared via version control. Option C (CLAUDE.md) is for project instructions and context, not command definitions. Option D describes a configuration mechanism that doesn't exist in Claude Code.

sample_questions.stem: You've been assigned to restructure the team's monolithic application into microservices. This will involve changes across dozens of files and requires decisions about service boundaries and module dependencies. Which approach should you take?

options.A: Enter plan mode to explore the codebase, understand dependencies, and design an implementation approach before making changes.
options.B: Start with direct execution and make changes incrementally, letting the implementation reveal the natural service boundaries.
options.C: Use direct execution with comprehensive upfront instructions detailing exactly how each service should be structured.
options.D: Begin in direct execution mode and only switch to plan mode if you encounter unexpected complexity during implementation.

sample_questions.rationale: Plan mode is designed for complex tasks involving large-scale changes, multiple valid approaches, and architectural decisions—exactly what monolith-to-microservices restructuring requires. It enables safe codebase exploration and design before committing to changes. Option B risks costly rework when dependencies are discovered late. Option C assumes you already know the right structure without exploring the code. Option D ignores that the complexity is already stated in the requirements, not something that might emerge later.

sample_questions.stem: Your codebase has distinct areas with different coding conventions: React components use functional style with hooks, API handlers use async/await with specific error handling, and database models follow a repository pattern. Test files are spread throughout the codebase alongside the code they test (e.g., Button.test.tsx next to Button.tsx), and you want all tests to follow the same conventions regardless of location. What's the most maintainable way to ensure Claude automatically applies the correct conventions when generating code?

options.A: Create rule files in .claude/rules/ with YAML frontmatter specifying glob patterns to conditionally apply conventions based on file paths
options.B: Consolidate all conventions in the root CLAUDE.md file under headers for each area, relying on Claude to infer which section applies
options.C: Create skills in .claude/skills/ for each code type that include the relevant conventions in their SKILL.md files
options.D: Place a separate CLAUDE.md file in each subdirectory containing that area's specific conventions

sample_questions.rationale: Option A is correct because .claude/rules/ with glob patterns (e.g., **/*.test.tsx) allows conventions to be automatically applied based on file paths regardless of directory location, essential for test files spread throughout the codebase. Option B relies on inference rather than explicit matching, making it unreliable. Option C requires manual skill invocation or relies on Claude choosing to load them, contradicting the need for deterministic "automatic" application based on file paths. Option D can't easily handle files spread across many directories since CLAUDE.md files are directory-bound.

sample_questions.stem: After running the system on the topic "impact of AI on creative industries," you observe that each subagent completes successfully: the web search agent finds relevant articles, the document analysis agent summarizes papers correctly, and the synthesis agent produces coherent output. However, the final reports cover only visual arts, completely missing music, writing, and film production. When you examine the coordinator's logs, you see it decomposed the topic into three subtasks: "AI in digital art creation," "AI in graphic design," and "AI in photography." What is the most likely root cause?

options.A: The synthesis agent lacks instructions for identifying coverage gaps in the findings it receives from other agents.
options.B: The coordinator agent's task decomposition is too narrow, resulting in subagent assignments that don't cover all relevant domains of the topic.
options.C: The web search agent's queries are not comprehensive enough and need to be expanded to cover more creative industry sectors.
options.D: The document analysis agent is filtering out sources related to non-visual creative industries due to overly restrictive relevance criteria.

sample_questions.rationale: The coordinator's logs reveal the root cause directly: it decomposed "creative industries" into only visual arts subtasks (digital art, graphic design, photography), completely omitting music, writing, and film. The subagents executed their assigned tasks correctly—the problem is what they were assigned. Options A, C, and D incorrectly blame downstream agents that are working correctly within their assigned scope.

sample_questions.stem: The web search subagent times out while researching a complex topic. You need to design how this failure information flows back to the coordinator agent. Which error propagation approach best enables intelligent recovery?

options.A: Return structured error context to the coordinator including the failure type, the attempted query, any partial results, and potential alternative approaches.
options.B: Implement automatic retry logic with exponential backoff within the subagent, returning a generic "search unavailable" status only after all retries are exhausted.
options.C: Catch the timeout within the subagent and return an empty result set marked as successful.
options.D: Propagate the timeout exception directly to a top-level handler that terminates the entire research workflow.

sample_questions.rationale: Structured error context gives the coordinator the information it needs to make intelligent recovery decisions—whether to retry with a modified query, try an alternative approach, or proceed with partial results. Option B's generic status hides valuable context from the coordinator, preventing informed decisions. Option C suppresses the error by marking failure as success, which prevents any recovery and risks incomplete research outputs. Option D terminates the entire workflow unnecessarily when recovery strategies could succeed.

sample_questions.stem: During testing, you observe that the synthesis agent frequently needs to verify specific claims while combining findings. Currently, when verification is needed, the synthesis agent returns control to the coordinator, which invokes the web search agent, then re-invokes synthesis with results. This adds 2-3 round trips per task and increases latency by 40%. Your evaluation shows that 85% of these verifications are simple fact-checks (dates, names, statistics) while 15% require deeper investigation. What's the most effective approach to reduce overhead while maintaining system reliability?

options.A: Give the synthesis agent a scoped verify_fact tool for simple lookups, while complex verifications continue delegating to the web search agent through the coordinator.
options.B: Have the synthesis agent accumulate all verification needs and return them as a batch to the coordinator at the end of its pass, which then sends them all to the web search agent at once.
options.C: Give the synthesis agent access to all web search tools so it can handle any verification need directly without round-trips through the coordinator.
options.D: Have the web search agent proactively cache extra context around each source during initial research, anticipating what the synthesis agent might need to verify.

sample_questions.rationale: Option A applies the principle of least privilege by giving the synthesis agent only what it needs for the 85% common case (simple fact verification) while preserving the existing coordination pattern for complex cases. Option B's batching approach creates blocking dependencies since synthesis steps may depend on earlier verified facts. Option C over-provisions the synthesis agent, violating separation of concerns. Option D relies on speculative caching that cannot reliably predict what the synthesis agent will need to verify.

sample_questions.stem: Your pipeline script runs claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" but the job hangs indefinitely. Logs indicate Claude Code is waiting for interactive input. What's the correct approach to run Claude Code in an automated pipeline?

options.A: Add the -p flag: claude -p "Analyze this pull request for security issues"
options.B: Set the environment variable CLAUDE_HEADLESS=true before running the command
options.C: Redirect stdin from /dev/null: claude "Analyze this pull request for security issues" < /dev/null
options.D: Add the --batch flag: claude --batch "Analyze this pull request for security issues"

sample_questions.rationale: The -p (or --print) flag is the documented way to run Claude Code in non-interactive mode. It processes the prompt, outputs the result to stdout, and exits without waiting for user input—exactly what CI/CD pipelines require. The other options reference non-existent features (CLAUDE_HEADLESS environment variable, --batch flag) or use Unix workarounds that don't properly address Claude Code's command syntax.

sample_questions.stem: Your team wants to reduce API costs for automated analysis. Currently, real-time Claude calls power two workflows: (1) a blocking pre-merge check that must complete before developers can merge, and (2) a technical debt report generated overnight for review the next morning. Your manager proposes switching both to the Message Batches API for its 50% cost savings. How should you evaluate this proposal?

options.A: Use batch processing for the technical debt reports only; keep real-time calls for pre-merge checks.
options.B: Switch both workflows to batch processing with status polling to check for completion.
options.C: Keep real-time calls for both workflows to avoid batch result ordering issues.
options.D: Switch both to batch processing with a timeout fallback to real-time if batches take too long.

sample_questions.rationale: The Message Batches API offers 50% cost savings but has processing times up to 24 hours with no guaranteed latency SLA. This makes it unsuitable for blocking pre-merge checks where developers wait for results, but ideal for overnight batch jobs like technical debt reports. Option B is wrong because relying on "often faster" completion isn't acceptable for blocking workflows. Option C reflects a misconception—batch results can be correlated using custom_id fields. Option D adds unnecessary complexity when the simpler solution is matching each API to its appropriate use case.

sample_questions.stem: A pull request modifies 14 files across the stock tracking module. Your single-pass review analyzing all files together produces inconsistent results: detailed feedback for some files but superficial comments for others, obvious bugs missed, and contradictory feedback—flagging a pattern as problematic in one file while approving identical code elsewhere in the same PR. How should you restructure the review?

options.A: Split into focused passes: analyze each file individually for local issues, then run a separate integration-focused pass examining cross-file data flow.
options.B: Require developers to split large PRs into smaller submissions of 3-4 files before the automated review runs.
options.C: Switch to a higher-tier model with a larger context window to give all 14 files adequate attention in one pass.
options.D: Run three independent review passes on the full PR and only flag issues that appear in at least two of the three runs.

sample_questions.rationale: Splitting reviews into focused passes directly addresses the root cause: attention dilution when processing many files at once. File-by-file analysis ensures consistent depth, while a separate integration pass catches cross-file issues. Option B shifts burden to developers without improving the system. Option C misunderstands that larger context windows don't solve attention quality issues. Option D would actually suppress detection of real bugs by requiring consensus on issues that may only be caught intermittently.
